group.passage:
In 2019, scientists exploring the deep sea off central California steered a remotely operated vehicle across the floor of a marine sanctuary, more than 3,200 meters below the surface. Suddenly the skeleton of a whale appeared in its lights. People watching the live stream online saw fish, octopuses, and worms crowding over the bones. The team had found a whale fall: the body of a whale that has sunk to the bottom of the ocean.
To see why such finds excite researchers, imagine life in the deep sea. It is cold and completely dark, and food is scarce. Most of what animals eat there is “marine snow,” a slow drift of dead plankton and waste from the waters above. A dead whale changes everything. Researchers have estimated that a 40-ton whale can deliver to about 50 square meters of sea floor as much food as marine snow would bring in 2,000 years.
Since whale falls were first studied in 1988, scientists have learned that a single carcass feeds a series of different communities. First, sharks, hagfish, and other scavengers strip away the flesh within months. Next, small worms and crustaceans move into the mud around the skeleton, which is rich with scraps of tissue. The longest stage comes after that. Bacteria break down the fat stored inside the bones, producing a gas called hydrogen sulfide, and other bacteria use this gas for energy. Thick mats of bacteria, along with clams and other animals that depend on them, can live on a skeleton for years or even decades.
Some of the strangest residents are worms called Osedax, a Latin name meaning “bone devourer.” Researchers came across them in 2002 while they were searching for clams in a deep canyon off California, about 3,000 meters down. The females have no mouth or stomach. Instead, they send green roots into the bone and release acid to dissolve it, while bacteria living inside the roots digest the fats. Fossils show that these worms were already boring into whale bones 30 million years ago.
In the deep ocean, it seems, almost nothing goes to waste. Long after a whale dies, its body goes on feeding a world that few people will ever see.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention “marine snow” in the second paragraph?

options.A: To explain how a whale’s body sinks to the sea floor.
options.B: To describe the main food of the Osedax worms.
options.C: To show that the deep sea receives more food than people expect.
options.D: To show, by contrast, how much food a single whale adds to the sea floor.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows, in the correct order, the stages of a whale fall described in the passage?

options.A: bacteria feed on fat in the bones → scavengers tear off the flesh → small animals feed in the nearby mud
options.B: scavengers tear off the flesh → small animals feed in the nearby mud → bacteria feed on fat in the bones
options.C: small animals feed in the nearby mud → scavengers tear off the flesh → bacteria feed on fat in the bones
options.D: scavengers tear off the flesh → bacteria feed on fat in the bones → small animals feed in the nearby mud

questions.stem: What can be inferred about Osedax worms?

options.A: They are usually the first animals to reach a whale fall.
options.B: They were discovered by scientists who had gone looking for them.
options.C: They could not feed on bone without help from other living things.
options.D: They began eating whale bones only after people started hunting whales.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organized?

options.A: It opens with a recent find, explains how a whale’s body supports life over time, and then turns to one unusual creature.
options.B: It compares two deep-sea expeditions and explains why the second one was more successful than the first.
options.C: It explains why whale falls are becoming rarer and then suggests what can be done to protect them.
options.D: It lists the animals found at whale falls in the order in which scientists first discovered them.

4.strategy_zh: 結構題先替每一段寫一個小標（開場事件→為何重要→分解階段→奇特生物→結論），再比對選項。只抓到兩個年份就說「比較兩次探索」是常見陷阱。

translation_zh.text:
2019 年，科學家在加州中部外海探索深海，操控一部遙控潛水器越過一處海洋保護區的海床，那裡位於海面下 3,200 多公尺。忽然間，一具鯨魚骨骼出現在潛水器的燈光中。在線上觀看直播的人看到魚、章魚和蟲擠在骨頭上。研究團隊發現的是「鯨落」：沉到海底的鯨魚屍體。
要明白這類發現為什麼讓研究人員興奮，可以想像一下深海的生活。那裡寒冷、一片漆黑，食物稀少。動物吃的大多是「海洋雪」——從上層海水緩慢飄落的死浮游生物和排泄物。一頭死鯨改變了一切。研究人員估計，一頭 40 噸重的鯨魚帶給大約 50 平方公尺海床的食物，相當於海洋雪 2,000 年帶來的量。
自從 1988 年鯨落首度被研究以來，科學家已經知道一具屍體會依序養活一連串不同的生物群落。首先，鯊魚、盲鰻和其他食腐動物會在幾個月內把肉撕光。接著，小型蠕蟲和甲殼類動物搬進骨骼周圍富含組織碎屑的泥裡。在那之後是最漫長的階段。細菌分解儲存在骨頭裡的脂肪，產生一種叫硫化氫的氣體，其他細菌再利用這種氣體獲得能量。厚厚的細菌墊，連同依賴它們的蛤蜊和其他動物，可以在一具骨骼上生活好幾年，甚至幾十年。
其中最奇特的居民之一，是一種叫 Osedax 的蠕蟲，這個拉丁名的意思是「吞噬骨頭者」。研究人員在 2002 年於加州外海一處深谷、約 3,000 公尺深的地方尋找蛤蜊時，意外發現了牠們。雌蟲沒有嘴也沒有胃。牠們把綠色的根伸進骨頭，分泌酸來溶解骨頭，而住在根裡的細菌則負責消化脂肪。化石顯示，早在三千萬年前，這種蠕蟲就已經在鯨骨上鑽洞了。
在深海裡，似乎幾乎沒有什麼東西會被浪費。鯨魚死後很久，牠的身體仍持續餵養著一個很少有人能親眼看見的世界。
